questions.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds  $2\,000\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\,\,\,\,2,\,2\sqrt{5},\,10,\,10\sqrt{5},\,…
$$

The first term that exceeds $2\,000\,000$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=2$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{2}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\sqrt{5})}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {5}^{(n-1)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\,000\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >2\,000\,000 \\ 2\cdot {5}^{(n-1)/2} & >2\,000\,000 \\ {5}^{(n-1)/2} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({5}^{(n-1)/2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2}\cdot \operatorname{log}⁡(5) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2} & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ n-1 & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)} \\ n & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}+1≈18.168.
$$

Therefore, the $19$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,000\,000.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >1\,000 \\ {2}^{n/2} & >1\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{n/2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000) \\ \frac{n}{2}\cdot \operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000) \\ \frac{n}{2} & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.001$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
64,\,48,\,36,\,27,\,…
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{48}{64}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.001.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.001 \\ 64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <0.001 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.001}{64} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1≈39.386
$$

Therefore, the $40$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.001.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <1 \\ 125{(\frac{3}{5})}^{n-1} & <1 \\ {(\frac{3}{5})}^{n-1} & <\frac{1}{125} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{5})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.008) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{5}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.008) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.008)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{5})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.008)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{5})}+1.\end{aligned}

\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.008)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{5})}+1≈10.452.

What is the first term that is less than $0.000\,000\,5$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\,\,\,\,256,\,64,\,16,\,4,\,…
$$

The first term that is less than $0.000\,000\,5$ is the
{{field-1}}th term.
questions.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=256$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{64}{256}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =256\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{n-1} \\  & ={4}^{4}\cdot {4}^{1-n} \\  & ={4}^{5-n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,000\,5.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.000\,000\,5 \\ {4}^{5-n} & <0.000\,000\,5 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({4}^{5-n}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5) \\ (5-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(4) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5) \\ 5-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}-5 \\ n & >5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(4)}≈15.466.
$$

Therefore, the $16$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.000\,000\,5.$

questions.problem: The $3$rd term of a geometric sequence is $18$, and the $6$th term is $486.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $10\,000$ is the{{field-1}} th term.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{3}=18$ and ${a}_{6}=486$, we can find the common ratio $r$ of the sequence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{n-m} & =\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}} \\ {r}^{6-3} & =\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{3} & =\frac{486}{18} \\ {r}^{3} & =27 \\ r & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{3}=18$ and  $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{3-1} \\ 18 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{2} \\ 18 & =9{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $10\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {3}^{n-1} & >10\,000 \\ {3}^{n-1} & >5\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({3}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1≈8.753.
$$

Therefore, the $9$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $10\,000.$

questions.problem:
The $6$th term of a geometric sequence is $\frac{1}{4}$, and the common ratio is $\frac{1}{2}.$ What is the first term of this sequence to be less than
$0.001\,2?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{6}=\frac{1}{4}$ and  $r=\frac{1}{2}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{6-1} \\ \frac{1}{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot \frac{1}{{2}^{5}} \\ \frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{32}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =8\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{3}\cdot {2}^{1-n} \\  & ={2}^{4-n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.001\,2.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4-n} & <0.001\,2 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡(2)^{4-n} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2) \\ (4-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2) \\ 4-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}-4 \\ n & >4-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
4-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.001\,2)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}≈13.703
$$

Therefore, the $14$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.001\,2.$

questions.problem: The $4$th term of a geometric sequence is $192$, and the common ratio is $\frac{4}{3}.$ The first term of this sequence to exceed $3\,078$ is the{{field-1}} th term.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{4}=192$ and  $r=\frac{4}{3}$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{4-1} \\ 192 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{3} \\ 192 & =\frac{64}{27}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =81\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =81\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $3\,078.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}81\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >3\,078 \\ {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >38 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(38) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(38) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(38)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{4}{3})}+1≈13.644.
$$

Therefore, the $14$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $3\,078.$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{3-1} \\ 200 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{2} \\ 200 & =\frac{25}{16}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =128\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =128\cdot {(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $8\,000.$
Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}128\cdot {(\frac{4}{3})}^{n-1} & >8\,000 \\ {(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1} & >62.5 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{5}{4})}^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})}+1.\end{aligned}

\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(62.5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{5}{4})}+1≈19.531.

questions.problem:
The $6$th term of a geometric sequence is $3$, and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$907?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that ${a}_{6}=3$ and  $r=3$, we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for ${a}_{1}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ {a}_{6} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{6-1} \\ 3 & ={a}_{1}\cdot {3}^{5} \\ \frac{1}{{3}^{4}} & ={a}_{1} \\ {a}_{1} & =\frac{1}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{81}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{-4}\cdot {3}^{n-1} \\  & ={3}^{n-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want $n$th term to be greater than $907.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{n-5} & >907 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(3)}^{n-5} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ (n-5)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(907) \\ n-5 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(907)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+5≈11.199
$$

Therefore, the $12$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $907.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the First Term Exceeding a Given Value
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds $2\,000\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
\dfrac 1 {32},\: \dfrac 1 4,\: 2,\: 16,\: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=\dfrac{1}{32}$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac 1 {4}\right)} {\left(\dfrac 1 {32} \right)} = 8.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{64}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{8}^{2}}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{-2}\cdot {8}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {8}^{n-3}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $2\,000\,000.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {8}^{n-3} & >2\,000\,000 \\ {8}^{n-3} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({8}^{n-3}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-3)\operatorname{log}⁡(8) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ n-3 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(8)}+3\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\, 000)} {\log (8)} + 3 \approx 9.643.
$$

Therefore, the $10$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $2\,000\,000.$

Example: 
                    Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
canonical_examples.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0. 000\,000\,1$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
16,\: 8,\: 4,\: 2,\: \ldots
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is $a_1=16,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac 8 {16}  = \dfrac 1 2.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =16\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & ={2}^{4}\cdot {2}^{1-n} \\  & ={2}^{5-n}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.000\,000\,1.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{5-n} & <0.000\,000\,1 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{5-n}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1) \\ (5-n)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1) \\ 5-n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ -n & <\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}-5 \\ n & >5-\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,000\,1)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
5 - \dfrac { \log (0.000\, 000\, 1)} {\log (2)} \approx 28.253.
$$

Therefore, the $29$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0. 000\,000\,1.$

                    Cases Where the First Term Is Unknown
canonical_examples.problem:
The $4$th term of a geometric sequence is $54,$ and the common ratio is $3.$ What is the first term of this sequence to exceed
$1\,000?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we are given that $a_{4}= 54$ and  $r= 3,$ we can use the $n$th term formula to solve for $a_1,$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{a_n&=a_1\cdot r^{n-1}\[3pt]
		a_4&=a_1\cdot 3^{4-1}\[3pt]
	54&=a_1\cdot 3^3\[3pt]
	54&=27a_1\[3pt]
	a_1&=2
	}
$$

So, the $n$th term of the geometric sequence is

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $1\,000.$ So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot {3}^{n-1} & >1\,000 \\ {3}^{n-1} & >500 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡(3)^{n-1} & >\operatorname{log}⁡(500) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(3) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(500) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(500)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(500)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (500)} {\log (3)} + 1 \approx 6.657.
$$

Therefore, the $7$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,000.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following geometric sequence: 

$$
3,\quad 6,\quad 12,\quad 24, \quad \ldots
$$

 

Suppose we want to find the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$ We can do this by creating and solving an inequality.

First, let's construct a formula for the $n$th term of the sequence. The first term of the sequence is $a_1=3,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac 6 3 = 2.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $3\,000\,000.$ So, we can set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >3\,000\,000 \\ 3\cdot {2}^{n-1} & >3\,000\,000 \\ {2}^{n-1} & >1\,000\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({2}^{n-1}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(2) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(1\,000\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(2)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

$$
\dfrac {\log (1\,000\,000)} {\log (2)} + 1 \approx 20.932.
$$

Therefore, the $21$st term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$

To check our answer, we can easily verify that $a_{20} < 3\, 000\, 000$ and $a_{21} > 3\, 000\, 000\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{20} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{20-1}=3\cdot {2}^{19}=1\,572\,864<3\,000\,000 \\ {a}_{21} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{21-1}=3\cdot {2}^{20}=3\,145\,728>3\,000\,000\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $a_{21}$ is indeed the first term that exceeds $3\,000\,000.$
